extracted.intended_audience: TeX implementers and advanced macro writers (experienced TeX users)
extracted.subtask_description: Technical guidelines for implementing TeX and writing advanced macros: character-code conventions, macro expansion/assignment semantics, list/verbatim programming idioms, and performance/resource cautions. Focused on making implementations and macro packages portable, correct, and efficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record format name and version
rubrics_metrics.description: The format name and version number are recorded in control sequences, in order to help the people who might have to explain why something doesn’t work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macro files like plain.tex should not be changed in any way, except with respect to preloaded fonts, unless the changes are authorized by the author of the macros.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a standard internal character code (ASCII-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: TEX’s internal code is based on the American Standard Code for Information Interchange (ASCII). There are 128 codes, numbered 0 to 127; TEX converts everything to a standard internal code when it reads a file and converts back when writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementations should provide the same internal code so macros and dvi output are portable across machines; express values in octal or hex when convenient (examples: ´142 or ˝62 for 'b').

rubrics_metrics.name: Make macro packages stick to standard ASCII characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Designers of TEX macro packages that are intended to be widely used should stick to the standard ASCII characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on nonstandard or host-specific characters in widely distributed macro packages to preserve portability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines for implementations with limited/extended character sets
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who implements TEX on computer systems that do not have 95 externally representable symbols should adhere to the following guidelines: (a) Stay as close as possible to the ASCII conventions. (b) Make sure that codes ´041–´046, ´060–´071, ´141–´146, and ´160–´171 are present and that each unrepresentable internal code < ´200 leads to a representable code when ´100 is added or subtracted. (c) Cooperate with everyone else who shares the same constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Appendix J for coordination (TEX Users Group). These rules help ensure that all 256 codes can be input and output when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support internal representation for 0–255 characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern keyboards allow 256 codes to be input, so TEX represents characters internally as numbers in the range 0–255 (´000–´377 or ˝00–˝FF).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementations may differ in which characters they will accept/output; a completely permissive version allows full 256-character input and output; other versions may restrict subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide control-sequence alternatives for missing characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems with fewer than 95 symbols can be used by invoking more control sequences; plain TEX defines \\lq, \\rq, \\lbrack, \\rbrack, \\sp, and \\sb so you need not type ' , ' [ ] ^ and _ respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macro packages should supply escape-control-sequence names for characters not present on the keyboard to retain portability of manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardwired character-code conventions TEX relies on
rubrics_metrics.description:
Very few conventions about character codes are hardwired into TEX; the important ones are enumerated: (1) INITEX initializes code tables as described; (2) TEX uses specific characters +-.,‘’"<=>0123456789ABCDEF in its syntax rules and uses most uppercase/lowercase letters in keywords; (3) 
umber, omannumeral, 	he, and 	ypeof produce certain characters; (4) \\hyphenation and \\pattern give special interpretation to digits and characters '.' and '-'; (5) codes for the characters $ . { } are inserted when TEX recovers from certain errors; (6) hexadecimal ^^00–^^ff convention is always acceptable as input when ^ is catcode 7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementers must ensure these behaviors are preserved so macros and formats behave consistently across implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map non-Roman keyboards to keywords or define equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: If TEX is implemented for a purely Cyrillic keyboard, the letter ‘Π’ should be assigned to code ´160 and ‘T’ to code ´164, so that ‘ΠT’ still means ‘pt’; or else define control sequences so TEX sees equivalent keywords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that system-specific character assignments preserve the character sequences TEX expects for its keywords, or provide macro-level mappings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the hexadecimal ^^00–^^ff input convention when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a special convention for representing characters 0–255 in the hexadecimal forms ^^00–^^ff; this convention is always acceptable as input when ^ is any character of catcode 7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form is especially useful when an implementer chooses not to output characters ≥128 directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand expansion vs assignment (mouth vs stomach)
rubrics_metrics.description: TEX’s control sequences are divided into two main categories, 'expandable' and 'unexpandable'; expansion of expandable tokens takes place in TEX’s 'mouth', while primitive commands and assignments are done in TEX’s 'stomach'. It is impossible to redefine a control sequence or advance a register while TEX is expanding a token list (e.g., during an \edef or \message expansion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design macros with this separation in mind. Use token-list registers or \\aftergroup and \\expandafter tricks when you need to perform computations that the mouth cannot do directly. Test with \tracingmacros=2 and \tracingcommands=2 to observe expansion behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \expandafter to alter expansion order
rubrics_metrics.description: The \expandafter\a\b construction causes \b to be expanded first, then \a; chained \expandafter can control arbitrary nested expansion order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful: \expandafter itself is expandable and chaining long sequences is error-prone; plan expansions to avoid excessive complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \aftergroup trick for variable-length token construction (with resource limits)
rubrics_metrics.description:
You can construct a control sequence that expands to 
 repeated tokens by using a sequence of \aftergroup commands; this method uses 
 cells on TEX's input stack and 
 on the save stack, so it may require a special TEX when 
 is large (e.g., >150).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer other methods when \n may be large; be aware of input/save stack limits and that \aftergroup-based techniques can be resource-consuming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider performance and output-size tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Different methods for constructing repeated material differ in speed and dvi output size. For example, using \cleaders\copy may seem fastest but can produce more dvi bytes per item than token-based methods; I/O time can dominate computation time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchmark and consider both CPU and I/O/dvi-size costs when selecting algorithms; for many asterisks, a one-byte-per-item method may outperform a seemingly faster box/leader method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use token-list registers for more efficient repeated expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Token list registers can be expanded more quickly than macros using \the and token-wise assignments, enabling faster constructions for some tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When performance matters, prefer token-list register manipulations to repeated \xdef or recursive macro-building where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of mouth's ability to do recursive operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Given suitably tricky macros (e.g., with \expandafter and sentinel tokens), TEX's mouth can perform recursive operations efficiently for some tasks without resorting to \aftergroup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study examples like the efficient deletion of the rightmost item from a list using sentinels to exploit mouth-time recursion; these techniques are subtle but powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design list macros with \{...\} and \\ separators
rubrics_metrics.description: List macros can be represented as \\{item1\\}{item2}... with \empty representing the empty list. Using \\ as a one-argument macro lets you 'execute' the list by redefining \\ temporarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide macros for left/right append, concatenation, lop (remove leftmost), selection by position, counting (cardinality), and centering (centerlist) by temporarily redefining \\; test for empty with \ifx\l\empty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect O(n) behavior for list operations unless special tricks used
rubrics_metrics.description: TEX does list-macro operations efficiently in the sense that running time is proportional to the length of the list; deleting the rightmost item in general cannot be done in O(n) steps maintaining full generality without using \aftergroup-like tricks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need removal of arbitrary positions with better than linear time, be prepared for more complex algorithms or resource tradeoffs; consider restrictions (e.g., unexpandable tokens) to get efficient deletion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain unordered sets via 'set macros' and test membership
rubrics_metrics.description: A set macro like \l = \\\alpha\\\beta\\\gamma represents {\alpha, \beta, \gamma}; membership tests and removal of occurrences (including \ifx-equivalent tokens) can be implemented with appropriate macros.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \def\\##1{...} scanning idioms to compare items; for removing equivalents, more sophisticated scans with sentinels and \edef may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \dospecials and \uncatcodespecials to disable special character behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: \dospecials is a set macro representing all characters that have a special category code; \uncatcodespecials can change all special characters to category 12 (other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is essential when you need to print characters verbatim (e.g., in listings), but be aware and adjust other category-dependent behavior (spaces, ligatures, line endings) accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct verbatim listings with careful \setupverbatim
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper \setupverbatim should include \obeylines (to end each input line with \par), \uncatcodespecials (so special characters print as themselves), and \obeyspaces (so spaces count), and also put line numbers via \everypar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pitfalls: (1) \obeylines changes ^^M to \active and \let^^M=\par but doesn't define ^^M, so modify \par before \obeylines. (2) \uncatcodespecials may change space to catcode 12 which interacts badly with \tt fonts; (3) \obeyspaces changes space to catcode 13 causing spaces to be affected by spacefactor. Remedies: redefine catcode 13 to be control space rather than using \frenchspacing, redefine \par (e.g., \def\par{\leavevmode\endgraf}) to preserve empty lines, and make certain characters active to break ligatures (e.g., Spanish ?‘ sequences). Test thoroughly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement \listing with grouping to restore settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Define \listing#1 as \par\begingroup\setupverbatim\input#1\endgroup so that \setupverbatim effects are local and restored after the listing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: the commands \input#1\endgroup will not be listed verbatim because they are read when \listing is expanded (i.e., before verbatim setup takes effect); plan accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle spaces, 'funny' spaces and active characters carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Space tokens can be implicit, explicit, or 'funny' (created via \uppercase and uccode changes). Distinguishing them is subtle; macros like \futurenonspacelet discard implicit/explicit spaces before scanning a nonspace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When implementing macros that accept variable numbers of arguments or need to skip spaces, use well-tested idioms like \futurenonspacelet; be aware that space normalization rules can change behavior (e.g., newly created spaces normalized to catcode 10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppress expansion for \write arguments when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: To write tokens to an external file without expansion, a macro (\unexpandedwrite) can insert \noexpand before each control sequence or active character so the argument is written literally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation uses heavy \aftergroup usage and assumes the tokens being written do not include implicit spaces or braces; token-count limits (≈150) apply due to \aftergroup accumulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: When testing token lists for a character, be mindful of nesting level
rubrics_metrics.description: A fast test for a character (e.g., '*') can detect it at nesting level zero but will miss occurrences inside groups; to consider all nesting levels a slower routine using \afterassignment and stepwise scanning is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the test appropriate to your needs: a mouth-time pattern-match for top-level tokens when groups should be ignored, or a full scanner when tokens inside groups must be detected; document limitations.
